lesson.title: Ask good questions
lesson.subtitle: Clear requests that help you learn

video.title: Ask good questions
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma looks over a student’s shoulder at his phone: a one-word request, “fractions”, and an answer that scrolls on and on. She tilts her head, unimpressed.
scenes.animation: The answer scrolls fast for 2 s; push-in on Salma’s tilted head.
scenes.narration: Yusuf typed one word into a chatbot: “fractions”. Back came three pages, and none of it helped with his homework. The chatbot had no idea what he actually needed.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name, the lesson title and the yellow AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to ask an AI for exactly the help you need.

scenes.visual: A chatbot box behind a closed door. Outside: a textbook, a classroom, a teacher, all out of its view. Only a typed line slides under the door.
scenes.animation: Items fade in outside the door; the typed line slides under it (1 s).
scenes.on_screen_text: It only knows what you type
scenes.narration: A chatbot can’t see your textbook, your class or your teacher. It doesn’t know your age, or what you’ve already learned. It only knows what you type. So a vague request gets a vague answer.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI chip. A prompt box fills with four coloured strips, one for each part.
scenes.animation: Each strip slides into the box as it is named (300 ms apart).
scenes.narration: What you type is called a prompt. A good one says four things. What you want. What you already know. Your level. And the form you want the answer in: steps, an example, or a short list.

scenes.visual: Split screen: on the left, the one-word request and its wall of text; on the right, the rebuilt request and a short, clear worked example of adding a half and a third.
scenes.animation: The rebuilt request types itself line by line; the short answer drops in under it.
scenes.narration: Here’s Yusuf’s request, rebuilt. “I’m in Grade seven. I can add fractions with the same denominator. Explain step by step how to add a half and a third, with one example.” Same chatbot, a much better answer.

scenes.visual: Three request cards fan out: a list (explain step by step), a light bulb (a hint), a question mark (quiz me). A student holds the pencil.
scenes.animation: Cards fan out one by one (200 ms); the pencil starts writing.
scenes.narration: Now the smart part. Instead of asking for the answer, ask it to explain step by step, to give you a hint, or to quiz you. Then you do the thinking, and the learning stays with you.

scenes.visual: A busy town. A traveller asks a stall-keeper for “the market”; he points vaguely down the road. Then she says where she is and what she needs, and he draws her a clear little map.
scenes.animation: Pointing arm wobbles; then a dotted route draws itself to the vegetable stalls (1 s).
scenes.narration: It’s like asking for directions in a new town. Ask for “the market”, and someone points vaguely down the road. Say you’re at the bus station, on foot, looking for the vegetable stalls, and you get directions you can follow.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds a maths worksheet with question four circled. Three request cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You’re stuck on question four of your maths homework. Which request helps you learn the most?

scenes.visual: The hint card gets a check badge. The student works through question four, then moves on to question five alone.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the worksheet ticks fill in one by one.
scenes.narration: A hint for step one. You still do the thinking, so question five won’t stop you. And if the hint isn’t enough, ask for the next one.

scenes.visual: A prompt box with a bouncer at the door: a name tag, a house, a phone number, a key and a photo are turned away. Only the maths question gets in.
scenes.animation: Each personal item bounces off the box (150 ms); the maths card slides in.
scenes.narration: One more thing: keep personal details out of your prompts. Your full name, address, phone number, passwords, and photos of you or your friends don’t belong there. Some tools keep chats and may use them to train later models, unless that’s switched off. Ask about the maths, not about you.

scenes.visual: A phone shows the lab: five ingredient buttons (role, task, context, format, language), a prompt strength bar and an ‘Ask the AI’ button. Each tap makes the example answer shorter and more useful.
scenes.animation: Ingredient buttons switch on one at a time; the strength bar fills (1 s).
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: build a better prompt
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll build a prompt from five ingredients: role, task, context, format and language. Its example asks for questions about the water cycle. Add one ingredient at a time, press “Ask the AI”, and watch the answer get more useful.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph stands beside a prompt box with three cards hovering over it. Answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Which of these should never go into a prompt?

scenes.visual: The phone-number card gets the check badge, then four summary lines tick in under ‘Remember’.
scenes.animation: Lines appear one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Four parts · Hints, not answers · Privacy
scenes.narration: Your phone number: personal details stay out. Remember: say what you want, what you already know, your level, and the form you want. And ask for hints, steps or a quiz, so the thinking stays yours.

scenes.visual: A student at home with a homework sheet and a phone, comparing two replies side by side: a finished answer and a short hint. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: The two replies slide in side by side; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: take one homework question. If you’re allowed to use a chatbot, ask it for the answer, then ask for a hint instead. Compare the two replies. Which one taught you something?

checkpoints.prompt: You’re stuck on question four of your maths homework. Which request helps you learn the most?

options.text: “Give me a hint for step one”

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a hint gets you moving and you still do the thinking, so you can do question five alone.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a full answer does the thinking for you, and a vague request gets a vague answer. A hint keeps the learning yours.

checkpoints.prompt: Which of these should never go into a prompt?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — personal details like your phone number stay out. The topic and your level make the answer better.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the topic and your level help the AI help you. Personal details, like your phone number, stay out.
